c.tagline: Maritime harbour city of seafood, sea shanties, and Titanic history.

taxi.fareNote: Uber and Lyft both operate in Halifax alongside metered local cabs, and ride-hail is widely available downtown. The airport run is often a flat rate of around C$68.

emergency.note: 911 connects to police, fire, and ambulance across Nova Scotia.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Late-night rowdiness around the downtown bar strip on Argyle and Lower Water streets on weekends warrants basic awareness.

hood_desc: The compact, walkable core running down to the Halifax Waterfront Boardwalk, home to the Maritime Museum of the Atlantic, historic Old Town Clock, breweries, and most seafood restaurants; the easiest base for first-timers who want everything on foot.

A trendy, creative district of Victorian rowhouses, indie coffee shops, craft breweries, and the buzzing Gottingen Street strip, plus the Halifax Seaport Farmers' Market nearby; suits younger travellers wanting local, hip character.
A leafy, upscale residential quarter of grand old homes near Dalhousie University, Point Pleasant Park, and the cruise terminal; a calm, green base a short walk or bus ride from downtown.

A busy shopping and dining street just uphill from the waterfront, lined with boutiques, cafes, and the Halifax Public Gardens; central and lively, good for shoppers who still want to walk everywhere.

The harbour city facing Halifax across the water, reached by a scenic passenger ferry, with its own waterfront, lakes, breweries, and a more laid-back, local feel; a quieter and often cheaper place to stay.
lodging: Muir, a Luxury Collection Hotel, Halifax
Hampton Inn & Suites by Hilton Halifax-Dartmouth

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink.

transit.hours: Buses run roughly 6am-midnight, with some later routes on weekends; the harbour ferries run about 6am-midnight (later on weekends).
transit.note: Halifax Transit runs the city buses and the harbour ferries to Dartmouth; there is no rail or subway system.
transit.pay: Tap a contactless credit/debit card or phone, or use the HFXGO app or a Tap card, on buses and ferries. One adult fare is about C$4.25 and includes 90 minutes of free transfers between buses and the ferry; exact cash fare is also accepted on board.

bus: Maritime Bus terminal (at VIA Rail Halifax Station)
ferry: Halifax Ferry Terminal (harbour ferry to Dartmouth)
train: Halifax Station (VIA Rail Ocean to Montreal)

transit.m: Maritime Bus airport shuttle to downtown (~40 min)
Halifax Transit Route 320 MetroX to downtown (~60 min)

tip.r: 15-20% at restaurants and bars is expected; tip taxis and ride-hail drivers around 10-15%.

food.name: Halifax Donair
food.desc: The official food of Halifax: spiced beef shaved off a spit, wrapped in warm pita with onion, tomato and a sweet garlicky condensed-milk sauce.

places.name: King of Donair
places.note: The 1973 original that invented the dish; still the benchmark for Halifax donair sauce.

places.name: Tony's Donair
places.note: Corner shop slinging donairs since 1976 and a perennial local favourite in the who-is-best debate.

places.name: Pizza Corner
places.note: The late-night intersection of donair shops that fuels downtown after last call.

food.name: Lobster Roll
food.desc: Cold-water Atlantic lobster, claw and tail meat lightly dressed and piled into a toasted split-top bun; Nova Scotia's summer signature.

places.name: The Bicycle Thief
places.note: Busy boardwalk restaurant whose lobster roll is a fixture of Halifax best-of lists.

places.name: Shuck Seafood and Raw Bar
places.note: Seaport oyster bar doing a straightforward, generously filled roll with local shellfish.

places.name: Tom's Lobster Shack
places.note: An hour out of town; whole claw and tail on a toasted sesame bun, often called the province's best.

food.name: Digby Scallops
food.desc: Sweet, plump Bay of Fundy scallops from Digby, usually pan-seared hard for a caramel crust and served simply with butter and lemon.

places.name: McKelvie's
places.note: Long-running seafood house in an old fire station, a reliable spot for seared Digby scallops.

places.name: Gio
places.note: Upscale kitchen that features Digby scallops on its seasonal Nova Scotian menu.

places.name: Sou'Wester in the City
places.note: Waterfront outpost of the Peggys Cove classic, strong on scallops and chowder.

food.name: Hodge Podge
food.desc: A late-summer Nova Scotian stew of new potatoes, baby carrots, beans and peas barely simmered in cream and butter; farm food, briefly in season.

places.name: The Wooden Monkey
places.note: Local-sourcing restaurant that puts seasonal Nova Scotian vegetable dishes on the menu.

places.name: Halifax Seaport Farmers Market
places.note: Saturday market stalls sell hodge podge vegetables and sometimes ready-made bowls in August.

places.name: Chives Canadian Bistro
places.note: Downtown bistro built on Annapolis Valley produce and changing seasonal plates.

food.name: Oatcakes
food.desc: Dense, crumbly Scottish-descended oat biscuits, lightly sweet and sometimes half-dipped in chocolate; the standard Maritime coffee companion.

places.name: Halifax Seaport Farmers Market
places.note: Multiple bakers sell traditional and chocolate-dipped Cape Breton style oatcakes.

places.name: LF Bakery
places.note: Acclaimed Halifax bakery whose counter pastries and oat bakes draw morning queues.

places.name: Alderney Landing Farmers Market
places.note: Ferry-ride market across the harbour with home bakers selling oatcakes by the bag.

food.name: Seafood Chowder
food.desc: Cream chowder loaded with haddock, scallops, lobster and mussels, thickened just enough to hold a spoon; served in every harbourside kitchen.

places.name: Salty's
places.note: Harbour-view institution on the boardwalk with a classic Maritime chowder.

places.name: The Five Fishermen
places.note: Historic downtown seafood restaurant known for chowder and its mussel bar.

places.name: Sou'Wester in the City
places.note: Casual waterfront room doing chowder, fish and chips and scallops all day.

food.name: Alexander Keith's India Pale Ale
food.desc: Halifax's hometown ale, brewed on Lower Water Street since 1820 and still ordered by name in every pub in the city.

places.name: Alexander Keith's Brewery
places.note: The 1820 brewery runs costumed tours ending in its own tap room.

places.name: The Split Crow Pub
places.note: Old-town pub with live East Coast music and Keith's on permanent tap.

places.name: Garrison Brewing Company
places.note: Seaport craft brewery taproom if you want a local alternative to Keith's.

food.name: Tidal Bay Wine
food.desc: Nova Scotia's appellation white: crisp, low-alcohol and high in acid, made to drink with the province's shellfish. Bottled by Annapolis Valley wineries.

places.name: Bishop's Cellar
places.note: Independent wine shop with the city's deepest selection of Nova Scotia bottles.

places.name: Obladee Wine Bar
places.note: Small downtown wine bar that pours Tidal Bay and other local wines by the glass.

places.name: Chives Canadian Bistro
places.note: Pairs Annapolis Valley wines with seasonal Nova Scotian cooking.

landmarks: Halifax Citadel National Historic Site
This star-shaped hilltop fortress, patrolled by kilted 78th Highlanders and firing its noon gun daily, has guarded the harbour since the mid-1800s.
Halifax Waterfront Boardwalk
One of the world's longest urban boardwalks stretches four kilometers past ships, seafood shacks, hammocks and the famous drunken lamppost sculptures.
Maritime Museum of the Atlantic
Canada's oldest maritime museum tells gripping stories of the Titanic recovery and the 1917 Halifax Explosion, with the CSS Acadia moored outside.
Canadian Museum of Immigration at Pier 21
Set in the harbourside shed where one million newcomers entered Canada between 1928 and 1971, this moving museum is the country's Ellis Island.
Halifax Public Gardens
A rare surviving Victorian formal garden from 1867 charms with wrought-iron gates, a candy-striped bandstand, fountains and impeccably kept flowerbeds.
Old Town Clock
Ticking on Citadel Hill since 1803, Prince Edward's three-tiered Palladian timepiece is Halifax's most enduring symbol of Georgian military punctuality.
Point Pleasant Park
Seventy-five hectares of forested trails at the peninsula's tip weave past centuries-old fortification ruins to breezy views of container ships entering the harbour.
Fairview Lawn Cemetery (Titanic Graves)
One hundred twenty-one Titanic victims rest beneath granite markers arranged like a ship's bow, a quietly powerful pilgrimage site since 1912.
St. Paul's Church
Canada's oldest Protestant church, built in 1750 on the Grand Parade, survived the Halifax Explosion, which embedded debris still visible in its walls.
Africville
A replica of the Seaview United Baptist Church housing a museum on the razed Black community of Africville, a National Historic Site on the edge of Halifax Harbour.

train.note: VIA Rail's overnight Ocean train runs several times a week from Halifax Station along the coast to Moncton, Quebec City, and Montreal (about 24 hours); it is the only rail service and is domestic only.

bus.note: Maritime Bus links Halifax to the rest of the Maritimes — Truro, Moncton, Charlottetown, and Fredericton — from the terminal at the VIA Rail station; there are no international bus routes, as the nearest US border is a long drive away.

intl.to: Dartmouth - Alderney & Woodside (Canada) - 10-12 min harbour crossing on a normal transit fare

ferry.note: The Halifax Transit ferry crosses the harbour to Dartmouth (Alderney and Woodside) in about 10-12 minutes on a normal transit fare. Seasonal Bay Ferries services from nearby Yarmouth run to Bar Harbor, Maine, but there is no direct international ferry from Halifax itself.

full.blurb: The picture-perfect UNESCO-listed old town of Old Town Lunenburg with its colourful waterfront and the Bluenose II schooner, about 1h15 down the South Shore.
full.name: Lunenburg

full.blurb: The Bay of Fundy's Wolfville and Grand-Pré wine country, with the world's highest tides and Acadian history, a scenic drive from the city.
full.name: Annapolis Valley & Bay of Fundy

half.blurb: The iconic wave-battered granite lighthouse and fishing village, Nova Scotia's most-photographed spot, under an hour from downtown.
half.name: Peggy's Cove

half.blurb: A string of white-sand surf beaches along the Eastern Shore, with boardwalks over the dunes and cold-Atlantic swimming in summer.
half.name: Lawrencetown & Martinique Beach
